subject: surgery
title: Perforated Peptic Ulcer, Graham Patch Omentopexy, and Gastric Outlet Obstruction

steps.tx: Peptic ulcer perforation represents one of the most common acute abdominal surgical emergencies. Perforations occur primarily in ulcers situated on the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum (D1) or the anterior prepyloric gastric antrum. In contrast, posterior duodenal ulcers rarely perforate into the peritoneal cavity; instead, they erode into the **gastroduodenal artery**, precipitating massive upper gastrointestinal haematemesis and hypovolaemic shock.
steps.say: Perforated peptic ulcers typically occur on the anterior duodenal wall, while posterior ulcers erode into the gastroduodenal artery, causing massive gastrointestinal bleeding.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic showing anterior duodenal ulcer perforation versus posterior erosion into the gastroduodenal artery.
vis.caption: Peptic ulcer complications: anterior duodenal perforation versus posterior arterial erosion. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The sudden rupture of an anterior peptic ulcer releases acidic gastric secretions, bile, and pancreatic enzymes directly into the greater peritoneal sac, inducing intense chemical peritonitis. Patients experience immediate, agonizing, knife-like epigastric pain that rapidly generalizes throughout the abdomen. On physical examination, the abdomen is intensely tender with involuntary muscle guarding and rigid palpation, classically described as **board-like rigidity**.
steps.say: Perforation leaks acidic gastric juice and bile into the peritoneum, causing severe chemical peritonitis with sudden agonizing pain and board-like abdominal rigidity.

steps.tx: Percussion of the abdomen reveals obliteration of normal hepatic dullness, caused by free gas escaping from the perforated viscus and gathering between the anterior surface of the liver and the abdominal wall. An erect chest radiograph confirms the diagnosis in roughly seventy-five percent of cases by demonstrating **pneumoperitoneum**, visible as a crescent of free gas beneath the right hemidiaphragm. If the patient is too unstable to sit erect, a left lateral decubitus radiograph demonstrates free air over the liver.
steps.say: Erect chest radiography reveals free gas under the right hemidiaphragm in seventy-five percent of cases. Percussion confirms loss of normal liver dullness due to intraperitoneal air.

vis.alt: Pneumoperitoneum: gas under the diaphragm on an erect chest radiograph.
vis.caption: Pneumoperitoneum: gas under the diaphragm on an erect chest radiograph. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: When plain radiographs are equivocal, non-contrast or contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen is the diagnostic investigation of choice, achieving sensitivity exceeding ninety-eight percent for detecting tiny retroperitoneal or subhepatic micro-pneumoperitoneum bubbles. Immediate pre-operative resuscitation prioritizes vigorous intravenous crystalloid rehydration, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering enteric gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, high-dose intravenous proton pump inhibitors, and nasogastric decompression via a **large-bore Ryle tube**.
steps.say: CT of the abdomen is the most sensitive test for detecting subtle free air. Resuscitation requires intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, high-dose PPIs, and nasogastric suction.

steps.tx: The definitive surgical standard for closing an anterior perforated peptic ulcer is the **Graham patch omentopexy**, performed via open laparotomy or laparoscopy. In the original Graham technique, the surgeon places three or four full-thickness absorbable sutures across the perforation without tying them, lays a vascularized pedicle of viable greater omentum over the defect, and ties the sutures gently across the omental buttress to create an airtight seal.
steps.say: Surgical closure is achieved using a Graham patch omentopexy. A vascularized pedicle of greater omentum is tied over the perforation to produce an airtight, healing seal.

steps.tx: A modern variation is the modified Cellan-Jones technique, in which the perforation edges are primarily approximated before securing the omental pedicle. Crucially, any perforated gastric ulcer must undergo a **wedge excision biopsy** of its margins before repair, because up to ten percent of apparently benign perforated gastric ulcers harbour an underlying malignant adenocarcinoma. Duodenal ulcers almost never harbor malignancy, so routine biopsy is not required.
steps.say: Perforated gastric ulcers must always be biopsied to rule out underlying gastric carcinoma, whereas duodenal ulcers are almost universally benign and do not require biopsy.

steps.tx: Following successful surgical repair, all patients must receive eradication therapy for Helicobacter pylori and complete a six- to eight-week course of oral proton pump inhibitors. In the era of potent acid suppression and H. pylori eradication, acid-reducing procedures like truncal vagotomy are obsolete in emergency ulcer surgery. Repeat endoscopy at eight weeks is mandatory for all gastric ulcers to verify **complete mucosal ulcer healing**.
steps.say: Postoperative management requires Helicobacter pylori eradication and proton pump inhibitors. Gastric ulcers require repeat endoscopy at eight weeks to ensure complete healing.

rows: Eliminates organism and prevents future relapse

steps.tx: Another classic mechanical complication of chronic, untreated peptic ulcer disease is **gastric outlet obstruction**. Decades of recurrent ulceration, inflammation, and scarring lead to dense fibrous stenosis of the pyloric channel or duodenal bulb. Patients present with persistent non-bilious vomiting containing undigested food eaten hours earlier, visible left-to-right gastric peristaltic waves, and an audible succussion splash heard over the epigastrium more than four hours after a meal.
steps.say: Gastric outlet obstruction arises from chronic peptic scarring at the pylorus. It presents with non-bilious vomiting of undigested food and an audible epigastric succussion splash.
